decisions.reason: The requirements cover different error triggers: handshake failure versus another TLS protocol error. The common termination outcome does not make those atomic checks equivalent.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the key_share extension are separate implementation capabilities.
The same forbidden extension is checked in different handshake messages: Certificate and CertificateRequest.
The same forbidden extension is checked in different handshake messages: EncryptedExtensions and CertificateRequest.
One check requires a server to emit a downgrade sentinel; the other requires a client to inspect a received sentinel. They apply to different roles and actions.

Both require the NewSessionTicket early_data extension body to be a uint32 max_early_data_size. The canonical requirement uses the direct Section 4.2.10 body definition rather than the appendix restatement.
These derive different secrets with different labels and transcript endpoints: exporter_master_secret through server Finished and resumption_master_secret through client Finished.
The requirements map different ContentType enum members to different numeric values.
HelloRetryRequest selected_group must satisfy two independent predicates: presence in supported_groups and absence from the original key_share entries.
Forbidding a certificate does not fully require the replacement value to correspond to the server's long-term key; these are separate constraints on the Certificate message content.
Key Usage bits and Extended Key Usage OIDs are separate certificate fields with different matching checks.
An unrecognized extension type and an unrecognized named-group value are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
The constraints apply different length ranges to different ClientHello vectors: cipher_suites and extensions.
One check defines the shared secret as the scalar-multiplication result; the other checks only the local-secret scalar input to that operation.
An unrecognized signature algorithm and an unrecognized extension type are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
The requirements encode different PskKeyExchangeMode enum members with different values.
Finished and CertificateVerify are different handshake messages, so their encryption checks are distinct despite using the same traffic-secret generation.
The supported_versions presence rule is applied to different message types: HelloRetryRequest and ClientHello.
The requirements encode different KeyUpdateRequest enum members with different values.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the supported_versions extension are separate implementation capabilities.
An out-of-range field and an incorrect encoded length are different malformed-message conditions, even though both produce decode_error.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the cookie extension are separate implementation capabilities.
The requirements constrain separate ClientHello fields: actual offered versions in supported_versions and the fixed legacy_version value.
One check requires sending supported_groups in ClientHello; the other requires using the received extension during group negotiation.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the supported_versions extension are separate implementation capabilities.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the server_name extension are separate implementation capabilities.
An unrecognized key share and an unrecognized supported version are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the cookie extension are separate implementation capabilities.
Empty and EndOfEarlyData are different protocol structures, even though both have zero fields.
Different Handshake.msg_type values select different message-body structures: Certificate and Finished.
The ContentType field belongs to different record structures and positions: TLSPlaintext and TLSInnerPlaintext.
An unrecognized key share and an unrecognized named group are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
Record-boundary alignment is checked for different handshake messages: KeyUpdate and EndOfEarlyData.
An unrecognized key share and an unrecognized signature algorithm are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the server_name extension are separate implementation capabilities.
Offering an obsolete_RESERVED group and negotiating one are different protocol actions and independently testable prohibitions.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the supported_groups extension are separate implementation capabilities.
Both require AlertLevel.fatal to encode as numeric value 2. The canonical requirement uses the direct alert protocol definition rather than the appendix restatement.
The derivation has separate required inputs: the handshake transcript and the handshake-established input secrets.
A defined Section 6.2 alert and an unknown alert are different received values and separate fatal-alert cases.
The peer public key as u-coordinate and the local secret key as scalar are separate inputs to the ECDH operation.
An oversized decrypted TLSPlaintext and an oversized received TLSCiphertext are different record-layer conditions, despite sharing record_overflow.
Different Handshake.msg_type values select different message-body structures: ClientHello and Certificate.
The key_share extension has message-specific bodies in ClientHello and ServerHello, requiring separate encoding and parsing checks.
Different Handshake.msg_type values select different message-body structures: CertificateRequest and CertificateVerify.
The placement rules apply to different extension types: server_name and supported_groups.
Different Handshake.msg_type values select different message-body structures: ServerHello and Certificate.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the supported_groups extension are separate implementation capabilities.
The placement rules apply to different extensions and allowed message sets: key_share and cookie.
The checks protect different endpoint identities against different attacker classes: client identity against passive and active attackers, and server identity against passive attackers.
Supporting rsa_pkcs1_sha256 for certificates and supporting ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 are separate signature-scheme capabilities.
The requirements mandate support for different cipher suites.
The placement rules apply to different extension types: server_name and server_certificate_type.
Omitting CertificateVerify when an endpoint is not certificate-authenticated and requiring it when a server is certificate-authenticated cover different conditions and role-specific state paths.
ECDSA signature support and secp256r1 key-exchange support are separate cryptographic capabilities.
The transitions belong to different endpoint state machines, and the server transition additionally depends on receiving a non-empty Certificate.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the signature_algorithms extension are separate implementation capabilities.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the key_share extension are separate implementation capabilities.
An unrecognized cipher suite and an unrecognized supported version are different ClientHello elements and require separate parser tests.
psk_ke and psk_dhe_ke are different negotiated modes with opposite key-share and key-establishment requirements.
Using MGF1 and selecting the corresponding hash for its digest are separate RSASSA-PSS parameter checks.
Supporting X25519 key exchange and implementing the supported_versions extension are separate implementation capabilities.
One requirement governs receiving an invalid zero-length Alert and mandates termination with unexpected_message; the other governs sending Alert records and forbids zero-length content.
Using MGF1 and selecting the corresponding hash for its digest are separate RSASSA-PSS parameter checks.

Both require TLS 1.3 elliptic-curve key shares to use each curve's single defined point format without point-format negotiation. The canonical requirement is the clearer rule in the key_share section.
Implementing a particular cipher suite and implementing the signature_algorithms extension are separate implementation capabilities.
